analysis.one_liner: Bans brand-name drug companies from paying generic makers to delay cheaper copies.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2019 with a sponsor and 21 cosponsors, the bill was referred to three House committees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic drug maker challenges a brand-name drug's patent, the two companies sometimes settle with the brand paying the generic to stay off the market for years — a practice called pay-for-delay. This bill would tell the Federal Trade Commission to treat such deals as illegal unless they truly bring the generic to market sooner. It would also hit violators with a 50% tax on the payments, block the companies from deducting those payments as a business expense, and claw back their research tax credits.
analysis.who_benefits: People who take prescription drugs. Banning pay-for-delay would let cheaper generic versions reach the market sooner, and generic drugs typically cost a small fraction of the brand-name price. Patients, employers, and government programs like Medicare that pay for drugs would all see savings when competition arrives earlier.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the FTC to presume that a patent settlement is an unfair method of competition whenever a generic filer receives something of value and agrees to delay research, manufacturing, marketing, or sales of its drug [S2][S3].

It adds financial teeth: a 50% tax on the amount paid under a violating agreement, denial of the business-expense deduction for such payments, and recapture of the research and development tax credit for violators [S3].
It requires company executives to certify to the FTC and Justice Department that all agreements related to a settlement — including side deals and oral promises — have been fully disclosed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug companies that use paid delay to extend exclusive, monopoly-priced sales of their drugs, and generic companies that accepted those payments instead of launching. Violators would also face civil penalties of up to three times the value gained.

drawbacks.text: The bill assumes settlements are suspect even when the generic maker would genuinely have lost the patent case; a company that challenges a weak patent and settles for compensation it deserves could face penalties, and the burden of proving procompetitive benefits falls on the settling companies [S3].

Applying the new penalties to agreements entered into after June 2013 — years before the bill — reaches back to past settlements under rules that did not exist when they were signed, which companies would challenge as unfair [S3].
If settlements become riskier and less available, more patent fights could run their full course in court, which can itself delay generic entry while litigation continues [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: stronger rules against paid delay would bring cheaper generics to market years sooner for widely used drugs, which is one of the largest sources of savings available in the drug-pricing system. The bill answers the main objection — that some settlements are legitimate — with carve-outs for early-entry licenses, reasonable litigation costs, and covenants not to sue [S3]. The main design weakness is the retroactive reach to 2013 agreements, which invites litigation but does not undo the public benefit of stopping paid delay going forward.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees and their subcommittees in February 2019; none of them held a hearing or voted on it, so it quietly expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on February 25, 2019, joined by 21 House Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Judiciary Committees, and then to the Health and Antitrust subcommittees [S5].
No committee or subcommittee ever took further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote appears in the action history [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021, without ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers keep the ability to pay generic competitors to stay off the market, preserving years of patent-protected, monopoly-priced sales — and consumers keep paying brand prices for drugs that could have had cheaper competition sooner.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its pay-for-delay ban, tax penalty, and FTC enforcement provisions.

against.name: House committee and subcommittee leadership (Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Judiciary)
against.role: Committees with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill in the full two years of the 116th Congress.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Companies that use pay-for-delay settlements to extend exclusive sales
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislative bans on pay-for-delay during this period; no record of this specific bill, so this reflects widely reported industry opposition to pay-for-delay restrictions.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 original sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored; the bill also received no Republican committee action before it died.

industries.note: Pay-for-delay settlements let these companies buy years of additional exclusive sales at monopoly prices before a generic arrives. The bill would ban the practice, tax the payments at 50%, block the deduction, and claw back research tax credits — directly costing firms that rely on paid delay to protect drug revenue. Their financial interest runs against consumers, who pay brand prices while cheaper copies are held off the market.

Generic companies lose the payments they received for staying off the market, but they also gain faster, clearer entry once paid delay is banned, and the bill preserves early-entry license settlements and reasonable litigation-cost payments. Some generic firms were on the receiving end of these deals; others compete better without them.
